title: Understanding the React Scheduler
body:
# How scheduling works > In one sentence: update tasks are sorted into two queues by whether they should be handled now (delayed vs ready); ready tasks are scheduled into the next macrotask through `MessageChannel`; execution is a loop that checks after each piece of work whether it should yield the main thread, resuming in the next macrotask if it does; and synchronous updates skip the whole apparatus and just run to completion. ## 1. A picture to start with Think of the scheduler as a restaurant's ticket system. React keeps producing update tasks (customers wanting to order); the scheduler decides who gets served first, when, and how long the work can run before the server takes a breath — that is, before it yields so the browser can handle interaction. --- ## 2. Step one: two kinds of task For every incoming task, the scheduler computes two things: - **`timeout`** — how much slack the task gets. The more urgent, the shorter. - **`startTime`** — the latest moment the task must begin. The split: | Case | Where it goes | |---|---| | `startTime` has not arrived yet (e.g. "handle this in five minutes") | **`timerQueue`** — delayed tasks, the waiting list | | `startTime` has arrived (it should run now) | **`taskQueue`** — ready tasks, the to-do list | --- ## 3. Step two: the ordering inside `taskQueue` Anything in `taskQueue` also gets an **`expirationTime`** (`startTime + timeout`): - **Smaller means more urgent.** - `taskQueue` is sorted by it, so the most urgent sits at the front and the closest to expiring is handled first. --- ## 4. Step three: how the page stays responsive — the core mechanism ### The problem If the scheduler ran each task synchronously the moment it arrived, the page would freeze and buttons would stop responding. ### The answer Schedule the work into the **next macrotask** instead of running it immediately: ```javascript // create a MessageChannel (two ports, port1 and port2) const channel = new MessageChannel(); const port = channel.port2; channel.port1.onmessage = performWorkUntilDeadline; // the function that does the work // calling this fires port1.onmessage in the next macrotask port.postMessage(null); ``` **Why `MessageChannel` and not `setTimeout`?** - `postMessage` is inherently asynchronous and runs on the next turn of the event loop - It is faster and more precise than `setTimeout(fn, 0)`, which is clamped to a minimum of 4ms > When the notes say "ready tasks are scheduled immediately but run in a macrotask", this is what they mean: not "run right now", but "queue it and arrange for the next macrotask to run it". --- ## 5. Step four: what workLoop actually loops over The function attached to `port1.onmessage` (`performWorkUntilDeadline`) is a loop, and each pass does this: 1. **Check `timerQueue`**: has anything reached its `startTime` (`startTime <= currentTime`)? If so, move it into `taskQueue`. This step is `advanceTimers`. 2. **Take the most urgent task from `taskQueue`** and run its callback. 3. **Keep asking "do I still have time?"** (`shouldYieldToHost`). If not — a few milliseconds have gone by and the browser needs to handle that click — **stop**, mark the work unfinished, and continue in the next macrotask. 4. Once the tasks are done, check `timerQueue` again for the next one due to wake. This is **time slicing**: instead of computing every update in one go, cut it into small pieces and leave the browser room to handle interaction in between. --- ## 6. What the task actually *is* **The scheduler neither knows nor cares what a task contains.** It is a pure queue-and-timer: whoever hands it a callback gets that callback invoked when it is due. The real rendering work — building the fiber tree, diffing — is a callback that **another React module, the reconciler**, hands to the scheduler: | Path | Goes through the scheduler? | Function (the name changed between versions ⚠️) | |---|---|---| | **Concurrent / async updates** | ✅ queued by the scheduler | React 16–18: `performConcurrentWorkOnRoot`
React 19+ (after the refactor): `performWorkOnRootViaSchedulerTask` | | **Sync updates** (e.g. `flushSync`) | ❌ never touches the scheduler; a dedicated sync queue | `performSyncWorkOnRoot` | > ⚠️ **Version note**: React later did a "root scheduler" refactor, adding `ReactFiberRootScheduler.js` and renaming `performConcurrentWorkOnRoot` to `performWorkOnRootViaSchedulerTask`. The role is identical; only the name and the file moved. If you cannot find the old name in a newer source tree, search for the new one. --- ## 7. Inside the scheduler (steps ④b, ⑤, and ⑥ of the full diagram below) ``` an update task is produced │ ▼ compute startTime / expirationTime │ ├─ startTime not reached → timerQueue (delayed) │ └─ startTime reached → taskQueue (ready, sorted by expirationTime) │ ▼ fire port.postMessage(null) │ (in the next macrotask) ▼ run performWorkUntilDeadline │ ▼ the workLoop: ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ 1. advanceTimers │ │ (timerQueue → taskQueue) │ │ 2. take the most urgent task │ │ 3. run its callback │ │ 4. shouldYieldToHost? │ │ yes → stop, resume next │ │ macrotask │ │ no → on to the next task │ └─────────────────────────────┘ [a completely separate path] sync updates (flushSync and friends) → skip all of the above → call performSyncWorkOnRoot directly → run to completion ``` ## How lanes relate to the scheduler > Lanes live entirely in the reconciler — specifically inside the `react-reconciler` package. > The lane mechanism never enters the scheduler, and the scheduler knows nothing about lanes. What crosses the boundary is the *result*: the priority a lane computes is translated into an ordinary priority number the scheduler understands, and that number does affect how urgent a timeout the task is given. The scheduler only ever sees the translation, never the lane itself. ## One complete update, end to end ``` ① setState() is called ↓ ② requestUpdateLane() — [reconciler] assign a lane to this update (what execution context are we in? an ordinary event? a transition? a sync case?) ↓ ③ scheduleUpdateOnFiber() → ensureRootIsScheduled() — [reconciler] - collect every pending lane on the root (getNextLanes) - translate lane priority into a priority number the scheduler understands - decide: is this a sync lane or an async one? ↓ ┌───────────────────┴───────────────────┐ ↓ sync lane ↓ async lane ④a call performSyncWorkOnRoot directly ④b the scheduler enters the picture for the first time: (the scheduler is never involved) call scheduleCallback(priority, callback) ↓ ⑤ the scheduler queues it, times it, waits for a macrotask ↓ ⑥ when it is due, the scheduler calls back into the reconciler (performWorkOnRootViaSchedulerTask) ↓ ↓ ⑦ [both paths meet here] — the reconciler runs beginWork/completeWork (this is where the DOM diff happens) ↓ ⑧ the commit phase paints it to the page ``` A fuller version is in #31, on the whole React render pipeline. ## ⚠️ Addendum: this `workLoop` is not the reconciler's `workLoop` The `workLoop` in section 5 belongs to the **Scheduler package**, and what it loops over are **tasks** in `taskQueue`. The reconciler package has its own identically-named pair, looping over **fiber nodes**: ```js // react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberWorkLoop.js function workLoopSync() { while (workInProgress !== null) { performUnitOfWork(workInProgress); } } function workLoopConcurrentByScheduler() { while (workInProgress !== null && !shouldYield()) { performUnitOfWork(workInProgress); } } ``` **So the line at the end of section 5 — "this is time slicing" — needs qualifying.** The Scheduler yields *between tasks*; what actually cuts **a single render** into pieces is the reconciler's `workLoopConcurrentByScheduler`, and that is only reached under particular lanes. The decision logic is in #23. ### The conclusion that matters: going through the Scheduler ≠ being time-sliced `DefaultLane` — everyday `setState`, `setState` inside `setTimeout` or `.then()` — genuinely is an async lane and genuinely queues in the Scheduler. But once the Scheduler wakes it, the reconciler computes `shouldTimeSlice === false` and takes `renderRootSync` → `workLoopSync`: **rendered in one go, never yielding partway**. The Scheduler only decides *when rendering is allowed to start*. Whether that render is sliced is a separate decision the reconciler makes from the lane.
